Purpose of the run

First country run of the controlled scaling phase (decisions E19 and E20, runs/rollout_plan.md). It applies the method validated in the North Macedonia alpha (RUN-2026-01) to Moldova, as a diagnostic covering the chain from EU requirement to priority, with a comparator step for the issues chosen at G6. It is also the first test of the shared multi-country architecture: what it teaches is reviewed before Montenegro (RUN-2026-03) starts

Scope Validated

Target country
Moldova (MDA)
Thematic scope
(a) All of Chapter 2, Freedom of movement for workers (Cluster 2, Internal market); (b) the technology and AI theme: recommendations materially relating to the areas listed in taxonomy/themes.csv (theme group TECH), wherever they occur in the accession material. Incidental references to technology are out of scope. The full analytical chain is followed for every issue originating from an in-scope Chapter 2 item or technology and AI recommendation. Material outside (a) and (b) is out of scope unless it is needed to follow the chain of an issue already in scope.
Time window
2020-01-01 to the evidence freeze date; earlier material only by logged exception where needed to understand the origin or evolution of an in-scope issue
Language
English primary; Romanian (ro) only for core relevant sources with no suitable English version, each recorded in the register; machine translation flagged and capped at Medium confidence unless a reviewer who reads Romanian is named. Russian-language material is not used unless approved as a deviation
Comparator scope
Chosen at G6 (procedure P4): two or three issues, comparators drawn first from countries already in the project, starting with North Macedonia's validated judgements

Issue-level judgements

IssueJudgementValueReasonStatus
RI-FMW-007@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and the only Chapter 2 sub-area wording among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files concerns legal alignment in general (2023) and the European Health Insurance Card (2025). The 2023 Analytical Report found no body responsible for enforcing the right to free movement of workers; Law No. 200/2025 gives the Equality Council that competence and the role of national contact point, as the Government reports in a machine-translated source, and the 2026 report confirms that the law entered into force in March 2026 to align with the acquis on workers' free movement rights. The improvement is legal only: the 2026 report does not assess the body, and the ten items of this run that name the Equality Council, all from the Government, concern its designation, staffing or planned measures, and none shows it at work for EU workers.Validated
RI-FMW-007@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedLaw No. 200/2025 is adopted and designates the Equality Council, which answers the 2023 finding in law. The amendment of the Equality Council law, the Council's restructuring and extra staff, training for public authority and Council staff, and information measures by the General Inspectorate for Migration are all still planned, and the Council had filled 19 of 33 posts (Government figures, machine translated). What remains is a body that in practice supports EU workers and informs them of their rights, with the mandate, structure and staff to do so.Validated
RI-FMW-007@MDApriorityLowThe missing enforcement body is raised only in the 2023 Analytical Report: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no later EU item on the Equality Council or an enforcement body, and no benchmark, Reform Agenda payment condition or key recommendation naming it. It is a specific acquis obligation within the chapter but not central to it, and the 2026 key recommendations address alignment and equal treatment of EU workers in general terms.Validated
RI-FMW-007@MDAtractabilityHighThe legal designation is done, and the remaining steps (amending the Equality Council law, restructuring and recruiting) are within the Government's control, with one lead body already in place. Staffing is the main constraint: the Council had 19 of 33 planned posts filled and its anti-discrimination directorate 4 of 7 (Government figures, machine translated).Validated
RI-FMW-015@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentSub-area wording on the European Health Insurance Card, which matches this issue, records no progress in 2025, and the finding that no national health insurance card exists because there is no integrated health information system is unchanged in the 2023 report, the 2023 Analytical Report and the 2024 and 2025 reports. In 2026 the Commission reports a finalised feasibility study and an approved EHIC Action Plan, which are planning steps and do not yet show a change in the card or the health information system.Validated
RI-FMW-015@MDAunresolved_gapopenThe 2025 and 2026 key recommendations still require IT infrastructure, systems and capacity for the EHIC scheme. Only the feasibility study is implemented: the EHIC module in the health insurance information system, the amendments to the health care and health insurance laws, the technical specifications of the card and the integrated health information system are planned or under development, and the Government states that the EU acts on the card are not yet transposed (machine translated). What remains is a national health insurance card and the IT, legal and administrative basis to issue and accept the European Health Insurance Card at accession.Validated
RI-FMW-015@MDApriorityHighThe EHIC is named in the Chapter 2 key recommendations of 2025 and 2026, and the finding that its domestic preconditions are missing is repeated in each report from 2023 to 2025, with no progress recorded in 2025. Issuing and accepting the card is a core acquis requirement for accession, which is why the issue is rated High although the key recommendation itself appears in only two reports.Validated
RI-FMW-015@MDAtractabilityMediumThe national health insurance company coordinates the work, the feasibility study is finished, an action plan sets a roadmap and the law amendments are planned for 2026. Against that, the card depends on an integrated health information system that the Commission found missing in each report from 2023 to 2025, and the insurer's IT directorate had 3 of 8 planned specialists (machine translated).Validated
RI-TEC-019@MDAdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceThis issue is not raised in EU material: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no EU item on consulting the data protection authority on draft laws or on following its opinions, and the four items on the issue all date from 2026 (the data protection authority's 2025 activity report and its machine-translated opinion on a draft law). One year of evidence gives no sequence from which to read a direction.Validated
RI-TEC-019@MDAunresolved_gapinsufficient_evidenceThis issue is not raised in EU material, so there is no EU requirement to compare against. The authority's own report shows that it reviewed 208 draft acts in 2025 and asked for changes to most of them, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item showing whether its advice on draft acts was then followed. What remains is to establish whether the authority's opinions are taken into account.Validated
RI-TEC-019@MDApriorityLowThis issue is not raised in EU material, as a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no EU item on it, which keeps its priority from being High, and its four items come only from the data protection authority. Consultation of the authority is a procedural matter at the edge of the data protection theme.Validated
RI-TEC-019@MDAtractabilityMediumConsulting the authority and acting on its opinions is a procedural step within the control of the Government and Parliament, and the authority already reviews a large number of drafts. Apart from the authority's account of years of unheeded requests to stop access to state registers outside the interoperability platform, a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item showing past progress or resistance on the uptake of its opinions on draft acts, so the rating rests mainly on the nature of the mechanism.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this issue concerns only part of Chapter 23. The 2024 report says justice digitalisation needs to improve, the 2025 report that the new Agency for Digitalisation in Justice needs faster operationalisation, and the 2026 report finds the Agency's capacity extremely limited and the use of IT tools across the justice system uneven and partial. The August 2026 amendments promoting digitalisation of some judicial procedures are recorded but not yet assessed.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MDAunresolved_gapopenThe 2026 report calls for further legal improvements and a decisive strengthening of the Agency, and a 2026 key recommendation asks for substantial progress on an integrated electronic case management system for law enforcement and prosecution bodies. The Agency exists but has extremely limited capacity, the August 2026 amendments are adopted, and the E-File application, which the Reform Agenda requires in all first instance courts by December 2027, is still planned. What remains is digital communication with courts in practice and connected IT across justice institutions, run by an agency able to deliver it.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MDApriorityHighDigital case filing in courts is a Reform Agenda payment condition (E-File in all first instance courts by December 2027), an integrated case management system for law enforcement and prosecution is a 2026 key recommendation, and justice digitalisation is raised in each report from 2024 to 2026. Both requirements are open and central to digital justice.Validated
RI-TEC-010@MDAtractabilityLowProgress needs courts, prosecution and law enforcement bodies to adopt connected systems, and the agency set up to deliver this has extremely limited capacity because of persistent staffing problems in 2026. Past progress is limited to setting up the agency in 2025 and the August 2026 amendments, and IT use remains uneven.Validated
RI-TEC-012@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Chapter 10 scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter: some level of preparation from 2023 to 2025 and moderately prepared in 2026. The 2026 report finds that the new legal framework reinforced the regulator's administrative and financial independence, and the Commission's 2026 release decision records access tariffs for the incumbent's infrastructure cut by 16% to 49% from 1 March 2026, against minimal network sharing (0.95%) in the 2025 baseline. The gain on independence is legal only, and an ITU finding reported in the Government's 2025 programme still describes independence and accountability as insufficient (machine translated).Validated
RI-TEC-012@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Reform Agenda requires at least 3% of the incumbent's infrastructure to be shared and network-sharing agreements by the incumbent; access tariffs have been cut and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act transposed in June 2026, but the agreements are still planned and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports the sharing rate after the 0.95% baseline. The law reinforcing the regulator's independence is adopted, and the regulator had filled 105 of 114 posts by March 2026. What remains is independence shown in practice and competitive safeguards that actually raise infrastructure sharing in a market where the incumbent holds more than half of broadband.Validated
RI-TEC-012@MDApriorityMediumThe Reform Agenda conditions on infrastructure sharing touch the competition side of this issue, but they are framed as implementing the Electronic Communications Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act, whose alignment belongs to the legal alignment issue. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found regulator independence in no benchmark, key recommendation or Reform Agenda payment condition; the Commission mentions it only in its 2026 finding that the new law reinforced it.Validated
RI-TEC-012@MDAtractabilityHighThe levers are legal and regulatory and within national control, and recent delivery is strong: a new law in force from January 2026, updated access tariffs in force within the Reform Agenda timetable, working arrangements with BEREC from 2025 and a regulator close to full staffing. The main constraint is market concentration, with the incumbent holding more than half of broadband.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Chapter 6 scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter. The 2023 report and the 2023 Analytical Report found company law not aligned on digital tools and processes, the 2024 report repeated the recommendation while recording a qualified electronic signature for filing with the business register, and the 2026 report records the new State Register of Legal Entities, launched in December 2025, which enables registration of all legal forms. The Government's own assessment (machine translated) is that the directive on digital tools in company law is only partly transposed.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe latest EU requirement, from 2024, is further alignment on the use of digital tools and processes in company law. What remains is full transposition of the rules on digital tools and processes, with company formation and filings fully online through the new register.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MDApriorityMediumDigital tools in company law appear in the 2023 recommendation and among many elements of the 2024 key recommendation on company law, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found them in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition and in no 2025 or 2026 item repeating the recommendation. It is a defined acquis requirement but a narrow part of Chapter 6; the Reform Agenda step on the new register is counted under the base registers issue.Validated
RI-TEC-035@MDAtractabilityHighThe remaining work is mainly legal and within the Government's control: a draft law on digital tools in company law is planned and the new register is in place. Against that, the register slipped from a planned July 2025 launch to December 2025 and online company registration still ran by e-mail as a provisional solution, so delays are the main risk (Government figures, machine translated).Validated
RI-TEC-020@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this is a cross-cutting data protection issue. Breaches are confirmed every year: 105 in 2022 in the 2023 report and 173 violations, given by CSO Meter for 2024 and by the authority's 2025 activity report for 2025, which may be one count reported for two different years; the 2025 report records a major health data breach, and the authority reports in 2026 that state bodies still access personal data through the COI technology. Rising complaints are read by CSO Meter as growing awareness rather than worse compliance, so they are not used as a trend.Validated
RI-TEC-020@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe 2023 requirement to train public servants and raise awareness has been answered by the authority's 2025 training campaign of 84 courses for over 3,600 people, and Law No. 195/2024, adopted and in force from 23 August 2026, lets the authority impose administrative sanctions directly. Sources conflict on data access: the Government says, in a machine-translated source, that data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, while the authority finds state bodies still using the COI technology outside it, and only about 50 public authorities had designated a data protection officer. What remains is compliance in practice by public and private controllers, including in health, with the new sanctions applied and access to state registers made traceable.Validated
RI-TEC-020@MDApriorityMediumData protection compliance is raised in the 2023 recommendation on training and awareness and in the 2025 key recommendation on health, which names the protection of personal data, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found it in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and not across three or more reports. Applying data protection law is central to the data theme, but the volume of authority and civil society material does not raise priority.Validated
RI-TEC-020@MDAtractabilityMediumThe new law gives the authority direct administrative sanctions, ending the duplicated procedures it blames for weak deterrence, and courts upheld its measures in 52 of 58 final cases in 2025. Against that, compliance depends on many public and private controllers, and the authority reports years of unanswered requests to move state bodies off the COI technology.Validated
RI-TEC-004@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this is a cross-cutting e-government issue. RI-TEC-004@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedMost shared building blocks are implemented and in use, but the human resources management system, which the Reform Agenda requires with at least three modules by December 2027, is still in development, the permits system was used fully or partly by only 16 of 31 issuing institutions at the 2024 audit, and the eArhiva system is planned. RI-TEC-004@MDApriorityMediumThe human resources management system is a Reform Agenda payment condition and is reported in each year from 2023 to 2026, but it mainly serves civil service management rather than shared e-government services, and the Commission records the shared platforms as in place.Validated

RI-TEC-015@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this issue spans several chapters; the 2026 Chapter 6 rating of some progress cites the new register and is context only. RI-TEC-015@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe 2025 and 2026 key recommendations require completing the digitalisation of the public property register, which remains in progress, and the Reform Agenda requires a digital cadastre covering 98% of the territory by December 2027; the legal entities register is implemented. RI-TEC-036@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Reform Agenda target of 75% of business services digitalised has been met, and EVO, the public services portal and 118 Unified Public Service Centres are in use; but in 2026 only 61% of citizen services are digitalised, only 133 of 414 business services run fully end to end, the Reform Agenda notes that the portal lacks integration with EU systems, and the link to the Single Digital Gateway is still planned. RI-TEC-036@MDApriorityHighDigital public services are the subject of two Reform Agenda payment conditions: the EVO Sign wallet integrating at least 20 e-services by December 2026, which is still open and shared with the electronic identification issue, and 75% of business services digitalised, which the Commission found met in 2026. RI-FMW-012@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this is only part of the chapter and the only Chapter 2 sub-area wording among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files concerns legal alignment in general (2023) and the European Health Insurance Card (2025). The 2023 report, the 2023 Analytical Report and the 2024 report all find that EU rules on supplementary pension rights of mobile workers are not incorporated into Moldovan law and that there is no occupational pension scheme, and in 2025 the government still describes the occupational system as at an early stage and plans full transposition of Directive 98/49/EC.Validated
RI-FMW-012@MDAunresolved_gapopenSources conflict: the Commission in 2024 says the EU rules are not incorporated into Moldovan law, while the government in 2025 says, on the basis of the financial market regulator's conformity tables, that the law is aligned with Directive 2014/50/EU and partly transposes Directive 98/49/EC. The responses named by the government, full transposition of Directive 98/49/EC and a draft amendment to Law No. 198/2020, are not yet adopted. What remains is incorporating the EU rules on acquiring and preserving supplementary pension rights into Moldovan law in a form the Commission accepts.Validated
RI-FMW-012@MDApriorityLowThe finding is repeated in the 2023 and 2024 reports, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on supplementary pension rights. Moldova has no occupational pension scheme, so the rules have limited practical reach, and the issue is a small part of the chapter.Validated
RI-FMW-012@MDAtractabilityMediumThe change is legal and lies with the government and the financial market regulator, and a draft amendment to the voluntary pension funds law is identified. Against that, the government and the Commission disagree on how far the law is already aligned, and no adoption date is given for the draft.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter; the issue's own items show change. The 2023 report and Analytical Report and the 2024 report find that no authority is responsible for open data policies, and the 2025 report finds Moldova not yet aligned with the Open Data Directive; the 2026 report records a law partially harmonising with that Directive, and the government reports a dedicated open data unit created in the economy ministry under Law No. 109/2025. The improvement is legal and institutional only: across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files the only measure of publication is the Government's count of 1,268 datasets on the portal, a single figure with no trend, and the World Bank found the portal still lacking in use in 2024.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe law on open data and re-use, its methodological rules and a two-person policy unit address the Commission's findings on alignment and on the absence of a responsible authority, but the law only partly transposes the Directive. The government itself says the data.gov.md portal needs updating and completing with data, the World Bank finds the portal still lacking in use, and the draft law on data governance has been suspended until 2027. What remains is full alignment with the Open Data Directive and related EU data rules, and regular publication and updating of datasets by institutions on the portal.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MDApriorityMediumThe Commission repeats the finding on open data in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the 2024 Growth Plan Communication refers to implementing the Open Data Directive, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on open data. Open data is a defined part of the data theme rather than its centre.Validated
RI-TEC-016@MDAtractabilityMediumRecent legal progress is recorded, with a law, methodological rules and a responsible unit in place, and the portal already exists. Against that, capacity is thin, with two posts in the ministry and one at the e-Governance Agency for the portal, and publication depends on many institutions, including local authorities, whose capacity the government lists as a challenge.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since this is only part of the chapter. The 2023 report finds 39 staff for 45 posts with high turnover, the 2024 and 2025 reports call for more capacity, especially staff, and the 2026 report says the authority's human, technical and financial capacities have not grown with its expanded mandate. The authority's own 2025 report gives 36 staff at the end of 2025 and a turnover rate of 18%, which confirms the finding but is its own account.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MDAunresolved_gapopenThe Commission's latest finding is that capacities remain limited while Law No. 195/2024 has widened the mandate, and the response aimed at capacity, strengthening the authority's administrative and human resources, has not yet been carried out. The authority itself reports pay below comparable supervisory bodies, staff overload and pressure on staff, and gives this as its own account. What remains is giving the National Centre for Personal Data Protection the staff, pay, budget and safeguards it needs to supervise independently under the new law.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MDApriorityHighAn adequately resourced and independent supervisory authority is a core requirement of the EU data protection acquis, and the Commission records the shortfall in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports with no increase in capacity recorded, which meets the test for High without a benchmark. The 2025 Enlargement Communication's call for more resources and independence for data protection authorities applies to all enlargement countries and only supports this.Validated
RI-TEC-018@MDAtractabilityMediumThe remedy is within the government's control, through the staffing limit, pay and budget, and Law No. 195/2024 was adopted. Against that, staff numbers fell from 39 in the 2023 report to 36 at the end of 2025 despite repeated recommendations, and the authority links turnover to pay below comparable bodies, which needs wider pay decisions.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter. The 2023 report asks Moldova to join the third-country trusted list and the 2024 report asks for interoperability with European Digital Identity Wallets; the 2026 report records amendments in December 2025 that fully align the rules for qualified trust service providers, joining the trusted list and cross-border testing of the national wallet. Use has not changed in the same way: the Commission gives 200 000 users, 9.8% of adults, in 2024 and over 266 000, 10% of adults, in 2025.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedRecognition has advanced through the December 2025 amendments, the trusted list and new identity cards carrying a qualified signature, but the Reform Agenda condition for December 2026 also requires an EU-aligned national wallet integrating at least 20 e-services, and the wallet was only started in September 2025, with remote identification moved to 2027. Use remains low, with about 10% of the population holding qualified certificates and fees of at least 11 euros a year reported by civil society in 2026. What remains is a working EU-aligned wallet, mutual recognition in practice and much wider, cheaper use of electronic identification and signatures.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MDApriorityHighThe national wallet aligned with EU standards, joining the third-country trusted list and alignment with eIDAS 2 are a Reform Agenda payment condition due in December 2026, and the Commission raised the trusted list and wallet interoperability in the 2023 and 2024 reports. Electronic identification is the centre of this theme.Validated
RI-TEC-026@MDAtractabilityMediumLegal and recognition steps have moved quickly, with Law No. 117/2025, the December 2025 amendments and the trusted list, and the work lies mainly with the e-Governance Agency and the trust service provider. Against that, use has stayed near 10% of adults, the eKYC deadline has slipped to 2027, and within the 2025 consultation another government body described EVOSign as still at the pilot stage and not ready for use in systems.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme. In 2023 the Commission finds no electronic biometric database and asks for planning towards Eurodac, and in 2026 it finds security and data protection weaknesses in the border police system and asks for interoperability ahead of a future connection to EU large-scale systems; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item from the 2024 or 2025 reports on Eurodac, VIS, ECRIS or other EU large-scale systems. Wider use of SIENA, which the 2026 report records, is the one change, and it concerns Europol's exchange channel rather than the EU systems in this issue.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MDAunresolved_gapopenApart from SIENA, the responses to the latest requirements are plans: interoperability of the fingerprint register with Eurodac, a national visa system interoperable with VIS, an analysis, by the end of 2027, of how to make the criminal records register interoperable with ECRIS and ECRIS-TCN, and a joint study with eu-LISA. The government reports a partial transposition of the Eurodac regulation in the fingerprint law, which is legal only. What remains is building or upgrading the migration, border and justice systems so that they are secure and ready to connect to Eurodac, VIS, ECRIS and the other EU large-scale systems.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MDApriorityMediumThe Commission repeats the call for data exchange through SIENA in the 2023 and 2026 key recommendations and raises Eurodac and EU large-scale systems in 2023 and 2026, but connection to most of these systems is expected only towards accession and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on these systems.Validated
RI-TEC-030@MDAtractabilityMediumThere is evidence of progress on SIENA, rolled out to several law enforcement bodies, and the government has a plan covering each system. Against that, the work needs the interior ministry, the migration inspectorate, the border police, justice bodies and eu-LISA, and the systems for Eurodac and VIS are still to be built or upgraded.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scales were not decisive, since this issue spans several chapters and is part of each. The main thread is taxation: the Commission finds no IT strategy for interoperability with EU tax systems in 2023 and 2024, records a programme prepared in 2025, and in 2026 records a roadmap for 2026 to 2029 while finding that EMCS and SEED solutions remain to be developed and that VIES interoperability must advance. The plans are adopted but no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files records a new connection to an EU tax or excise system, and the 2026 report adds that Moldova is not yet in ECURIE or EURDEP.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MDAunresolved_gapopenSome connections exist, such as access to TED since 2020, trademark data in EUIPO systems and use of TRACES, but they lie outside the latest requirements. The responses to those requirements are a tax IT programme and roadmap that are adopted, and connections to the CCN gateway, VIES and other tax systems, TESTA and IMI that are planned. What remains is building and connecting the tax, excise, radiological, civil protection and internal market systems to the EU systems the Commission names.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MDApriorityMediumTax interoperability is a core acquis requirement raised in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, but the Commission records good progress in the taxation chapter in 2025 and 2026, so the test for High on lack of progress is not met. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on it: the Reform Agenda's tax objective refers to EU taxation IT systems, but its step concerns taxpayer services. The issue groups many sectors, each with one or two items.Validated
RI-TEC-032@MDAtractabilityMediumThe tax service now has an approved IT programme and a roadmap with a timetable, which is evidence of planning progress. Against that, the work spreads across many agencies and EU systems, and some connections depend on EU arrangements open only to Member States, as the government notes for the AGORA system.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MDAdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceThe chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme and its items sit in the economic sections. The Commission finds digitalisation lagging behind in 2023, slowly improving in 2024, steadily advancing in 2025 and continuing to advance in 2026, but these findings concern the economy as a whole. Across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the only repeated measure of business adoption is the Government's share of enterprises making web sales, 0.9% both in its 2023 strategy and as the baseline of its 2025 programme, so no item shows a change in business adoption itself.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedResponses are in place: SME digitalisation programmes, association to the Digital Europe Programme and the first European Digital Innovation Hub, launched in April 2026. Against that, the Reform Agenda finds the share of businesses using digital services low, and the government's 2025 programme still gives a baseline of 0.9% of enterprises making web sales. What remains is wider adoption of digital technologies by small businesses and greater use of EU programmes and the new innovation hub.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MDApriorityLowThe Commission's findings on this issue are general statements in the economic sections, positive since 2024, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on business adoption. Business adoption is not an acquis requirement.Validated
RI-TEC-033@MDAtractabilityMediumSupport programmes, EU funding routes and the first innovation hub exist, and the Commission records steady progress in digitalisation. Against that, adoption depends on many small firms, and the government cites lack of knowledge, high costs and perceived long-term returns as barriers.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter. The Commission finds about 40% of mapped services available digitally in 2024, over 50% in 2025 with 64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024, and 82% of business services and 61% of citizen services by June 2026, and its 2026 release decision confirms that the Reform Agenda objective of 75% of business services was met. The 2026 report also finds that user uptake increased significantly, including in rural areas.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe business services reform is in place, with the State Register of Legal Units launched in December 2025 and the life events methodology approved, and the Commission judges the payment step satisfactorily fulfilled. Still, only 133 of the 414 business services counted are fully digital end to end, citizen services lag at 61%, the Commission noted low demand in 2025, and the systems of the entrepreneurship agency and the employment agency are still being procured or built. What remains is end-to-end online delivery and wider use of sector services, especially for citizens and in agencies such as the entrepreneurship and employment agencies.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MDApriorityHighDigital services for businesses are the subject of key recommendations in four reports: digitalising processes to cut administrative burden in 2023 and 2024, and digitalising the entrepreneurship agency's processes in 2025 and 2026. The related Reform Agenda payment step (75% of business services digitalised, with the State Register of Legal Units and the life events methodology) is met, so the rating rests on the repeated recommendations; online public services are central to the digital government theme.Validated
RI-TEC-037@MDAtractabilityHighThere is strong evidence of past progress, with the share of business services online rising each year from 2024 to 2026 and the payment step met. The work is led by the e-Governance Agency and the State Chancellery with shared platforms, although sector agencies and rural demand still need attention.Validated
RI-TEC-038@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme. The Commission finds the e-procurement system inadequate in 2021, calls for it to be overhauled or re-engineered in 2023, describes MTender as outdated in 2025, and in 2026 records limited progress on digitalising procurement and an outdated MTender that limits monitoring; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item from the 2024 report on e-procurement.Validated
RI-TEC-038@MDAunresolved_gapopenThe new system is still being procured: technical specifications were received in September 2025 and the call for bids was published in December 2025 with a deadline in February 2026, while the Reform Agenda sets a pilot of the new system by December 2027. MTender remains in use without planning, contract management and some procedures. What remains is designing, building and putting into operation a new e-procurement system that covers every procedure and stage of the procurement cycle.Validated
RI-TEC-038@MDApriorityHighThe new e-procurement system is a Reform Agenda payment condition, recalled in the 2025 release decision, and the Commission calls for it in the 2023 report and in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports. It is central to digital public procurement.Validated
RI-TEC-038@MDAtractabilityMediumFunding from international partners is secured, a concept and programme exist, and procurement of the system has started with World Bank review. Against that, the system has been called for since 2021 with limited progress recorded in 2026, and building a full new system is a large technical project.Validated
RI-FMW-008@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Chapter 2 rating covers more than this issue and is context only, but its progress statements of 2024, 2025 and 2026 turn on the bilateral social security agreements, moving from limited progress in 2023 and 2024 to good progress in 2025 and 2026. The issue's own items show agreements added in each year: Spain signed and Greece in force by 2023, Spain and Latvia in force in 2024, Italy and France signed in October 2024 and March 2025, Italy in force in September 2025 and Slovakia signed in March 2026.Validated
RI-FMW-008@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Commission asked in each report from 2023 to 2026 for further social security coordination agreements with Member States, adding in 2026 a request for gap analyses on the coordination regulations, and it reports in 2026 that negotiations with other Member States should continue. The Government reported in 2025 agreements with 17 of the 27 Member States, its own count, and the Slovakia agreement signed in March 2026 is not yet reported in force. What remains is agreements with the Member States not yet covered, entry into force of those signed, and the gap analyses on the coordination regulations.Validated
RI-FMW-008@MDApriorityHighConcluding further agreements with Member States is a key recommendation in all four Commission reports from 2023 to 2026, and the Chapter 2 progress statements of 2024 to 2026 rest on it, so it is central to the chapter. RI-FMW-008@MDAtractabilityMediumThe Commission records agreements signed or brought into force in every year from 2023 to 2026, negotiated by an established institution, the National Social Insurance House. The Government itself says it cannot commit to a number of agreements because the pace depends on the political will of the other states, so completion is not in Moldova's hands alone.Validated
RI-FMW-004@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Chapter 2 rating covers more than this issue and is context only. The 2023 report and Analytical Report found the preparatory work for EURES not completed, the 2024 report recorded its start with an action plan and the National Employment Agency designated as coordination body, and the 2025 report recorded a EURES department and the September 2025 Government Decision setting the national legal framework. RI-FMW-004@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Commission asked in 2023, 2024 and 2025 for the preparatory work for EURES to continue, and in 2026 it records the legal framework, coordination office and admission procedure as in place. RI-FMW-004@MDApriorityHighPreparing to join EURES is a key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the 2026 key recommendation asks for the measures, capacity and IT systems needed for full participation in EURES, while the Commission states that the previous year's recommendations remain valid. RI-FMW-004@MDAtractabilityHighThe work lies mainly with one body, the National Employment Agency, and uses Government Decisions and agency orders; the steps planned in 2024 and 2025 were reported as taken by the Commission in the following report. RI-FMW-011@MDAdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceAcross all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the EU items on the European Health Insurance Card concern its domestic preconditions: the 2025 sub-area wording records no progress on the Card and the 2026 report a feasibility study and an action plan, and these are used for the issue on those preconditions. RI-FMW-011@MDAunresolved_gapopenThe Government stated in 2025 that the EU acts on the European Health Insurance Card are not transposed and listed applying the Card and a draft law on cross-border medical care as planned. RI-FMW-011@MDApriorityMediumThe Card is part of the Chapter 2 acquis on social security coordination and is named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, as IT infrastructure and capacity for the EHIC scheme to be developed alongside the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information. RI-FMW-011@MDAtractabilityMediumPreparation has started: a feasibility study on the Card's impact on public finances was completed and a draft law on cross-border medical care is planned. RI-TEC-021@MDAdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceThe issue rests on a single item, found by a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files for personal data in elections and campaigns: a 2026 civil society report that illegal surveys in the parliamentary election campaign used personal data databases of unclear origin. RI-TEC-021@MDAunresolved_gapinsufficient_evidenceThe single item is a civil society finding, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files states an EU requirement on it or describes an intervention responding to it, so the gap cannot be measured against what the EU requires. RI-TEC-021@MDApriorityLowThe issue is raised only by one civil society source, the single item on it among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, and not in EU material, which keeps priority from being High. With no EU recommendation or benchmark, it is Low.Validated
RI-TEC-021@MDAtractabilityinsufficient_evidenceThe single item names no responsible institution and no past action on the issue, so how realistic progress would be cannot be judged.Validated

RI-TEC-039@MDApriorityMediumAccessibility of public sector websites and applications is a key recommendation in the 2026 report, the first Commission report to raise it in a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, and no Reform Agenda payment condition names it. RI-TEC-024@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentSub-area wording on the 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, which matches this issue, recorded no progress in 2024. RI-TEC-029@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe 2026 report asks Moldova to adopt the Customs Code amendments that give the legal basis for EU-interoperable IT systems and to advance the national customs IT programme approved in October 2025, of whose 25 systems three are operational. RI-TEC-029@MDAtractabilityHighThe Customs Service delivered the transit system, Convention accession and the Customs Decisions System close to the dates set, the Commission judged the related Reform Agenda steps satisfactorily fulfilled, and EU expert support continues. RI-TEC-001@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Chapter 10 scale is context only, as this issue is part of the AI theme and the scale was not decisive. RI-TEC-025@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Chapter 10 scale is context only. RI-TEC-022@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Chapter 10 scale is context only. The 2023 report recorded adoption of the Law on cybersecurity but said implementation had to start, the 2024 and 2025 reports recorded implementing Government Decisions aimed at NIS 2 alignment, and the 2026 report records further secondary legislation and the National Cybersecurity Programme 2026-2030 adopted in December 2025, replacing the strategy the Reform Agenda had described as lapsed. The improvement is mainly legal and strategic, as the Reform Agenda still found no holistic framework in 2025.Validated
RI-TEC-022@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe key recommendation of 2024, 2025 and 2026 asks Moldova to align legislation with EU cybersecurity standards. The Government describes Law No. 48/2023 as only partially harmonising with NIS 2, and the amending law for NIS 2, the laws on the Cyber Resilience Act and cybersecurity certification and the related authority designations were still planned in 2025 and 2026. What remains is full transposition of NIS 2 and of the Cyber Resilience Act and certification framework, with the authorities designated to apply them.Validated
RI-TEC-022@MDApriorityHighAlignment with EU cybersecurity standards is in the key recommendation of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and NIS 2 alignment with clarified institutional roles is part of the Reform Agenda. The legal framework is central to the cybersecurity theme.Validated
RI-TEC-022@MDAtractabilityMediumMoldova has adopted the main law and a series of implementing Government Decisions since 2023, which shows legislative capacity. The Cybersecurity Agency reports that missing staff and an incomplete framework limited supervision in 2025, the ministry's cybersecurity unit has four posts with one vacant, and the Reform Agenda expects compliance costs to meet resistance from operators.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Chapter 10 scale is context only. In 2021 the national CERT was pending approval of its mandate, in 2024 and 2025 the Commission asked for further effort on the operational capacity of the new Cybersecurity Agency, and the Reform Agenda found it short of staff, IT resources and legal authority. In 2026 the Commission reports the Agency operational as single point of contact and national CERT, with 32 staff by December 2025 and an incident platform in use, and judged the related Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe Reform Agenda step on making the Agency fully operational with a national CERT is judged fulfilled, but the Agency's 2025 report says supervision was only partly carried out for lack of staff and a complete framework, its SIEM and incident playbooks were incomplete, and it lacks qualified IT specialists. The Government reports that cyber incidents rose by over 30 percent between 2021 and 2023, and the 2026 report notes security vulnerabilities in the border police information system. What remains is enough qualified staff and tools for the Agency and CERT to supervise providers and protect state systems.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MDApriorityMediumOperational capacity of the Agency was named in the 2024 and 2025 reports and in a Reform Agenda step, but the Commission judged that step satisfactorily fulfilled, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no 2026 Commission recommendation on the Agency's capacity. A fulfilled condition with no repeat of the requirement in 2026 does not on its own make the issue High, although it stays central to the cybersecurity theme.Validated
RI-TEC-023@MDAtractabilityMediumThe Agency went from its launch in 2024 to an operational CERT in 2025, with substantial EU and bilateral support in experts, equipment, software and training. The Agency names recruitment of qualified specialists and limited own resources for equipment as its constraints.Validated
RI-FMW-001@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe Commission's 2023 analytical report found that the law on access to the labour market made no difference between EU workers and other third-country nationals, and the 2024 report recorded amendments letting EU citizens work without a work permit. The 2025 report recorded a law of July 2025 giving EU citizens a separate regime, and the 2026 report the entry into force in March 2026 of the law on free movement and residence of EU citizens, aimed at alignment; the improvement is legal only. The chapter rating (early stage in 2023 and 2024, some level in 2025, between some and moderate in 2026) covers the whole chapter and was used as context only.Validated
RI-FMW-001@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedLaw No. 200/2025, in force since March 2026, gives EU citizens a regime separate from other foreigners and, by the government's account, equal treatment with nationals, but the 2026 key recommendation still asks for continued alignment on access to the labour market and equal treatment of EU workers. The amendments to the employment law and its implementing decision, the adjustment of secondary legislation by several ministries and the removal of the citizenship condition for staff of private employment agencies are still at draft or planning stage. What remains is secondary and sectoral legislation giving EU workers equal access to employment services, active measures, service housing and private placement, and its application in practice.Validated
RI-FMW-001@MDApriorityMediumAccess for EU citizens to the labour market and equal treatment are central to the chapter and are named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, but not in those of 2023 or 2024, so the test of three or more reports is not met. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on the issue; the 2023 report also contains a general call to align legislation with the acquis, outside its key recommendations.Validated
RI-FMW-001@MDAtractabilityHighThe remaining work is national legislation and staff training led by the Ministry of Labour and other ministries, and the drafts are already prepared and under consultation. Past progress is clear: the Commission reports amendments in force from January 2024 and Law No. 200/2025 in force from March 2026.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingIn 2023 the Commission found that EU citizens needed a temporary residence permit for work and that their family members were treated as other foreigners, while the 2023 report recorded amendments easing temporary residence for EU citizens; the 2024 report recorded amendments in force from January 2024 letting them work without a work permit. The 2025 report recorded a separate regime for EU citizens, and the 2026 report the entry into force of the free movement law in March 2026 and a standard operating procedure for their residence documents; the improvement is mainly legal. The chapter rating covers the whole chapter and was used as context only.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedUnder Law No. 200/2025 EU citizens need no work authorisation and, for stays over 90 days, a residence card not tied to a purpose, but the Commission reports that only 28 applications for the new residence documents had been submitted after the March 2026 procedure, while 422 EU citizens were still to be documented under the old stay-for-work regime in 2025. Full separation of the two regimes in the general law on foreigners depends on a draft law due to apply from 1 June 2027, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs' secondary legislation on registering EU citizens is still being revised. What remains is the practical move of EU citizens and their family members to the new residence cards and the completion of the implementing rules.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MDApriorityMediumWork permits and residence conditions for EU workers are central to the chapter, but they are not named separately in a key recommendation; the 2025 and 2026 key recommendations on access for EU citizens to the labour market can be read as covering them, which would still make only two reports. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on the issue.Validated
RI-FMW-002@MDAtractabilityMediumThe legal change has been made and the General Inspectorate for Migration has an operating procedure, so what is left is mostly administrative and within national control. Few EU citizens had applied for the new documents by 2026, and full separation of the regimes depends on a new foreigners law that is still a draft, so progress depends on the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Inspectorate following through.Validated
RI-FMW-005@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingThe issue is first raised in the Commission's 2025 key recommendation to reinforce the employment service's IT infrastructure for EURES, when the 2025 report also recorded a new EURES department with a designated officer from January 2025. The 2026 report records technical standards for matching vacancies and CVs with the EURES portal and a new integrated information system developed in December 2025, aiming at fully digitalised services by 2027, while widening the recommendation to systems for EESSI and the EHIC. The chapter rating was not decisive, as the issue is only part of the chapter.Validated
RI-FMW-005@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe employment agency has a Labour Migration and EURES directorate (five of six posts filled) and technical standards for exchange with the EURES portal, but the interoperability of its information system with EURES, staff training on EURES and the rules on personal data in that exchange are still planned. The agency's own reports for 2024 and 2025 say it lacks a modern information system, and the new system, funded through the EU Delegation, is still being developed. What remains is a working connection between the agency's information system and the EURES platform, operated by trained staff, before accession.Validated
RI-FMW-005@MDApriorityMediumThe employment service's IT capacity for EURES is named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, two reports, and supports a chapter requirement that applies from accession. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on it.Validated
RI-FMW-005@MDAtractabilityMediumThe work sits mainly with one agency, which has already set up a EURES directorate and technical standards, so there is evidence of past progress. The new information system depends on external funding and on technical connection work that is still planned, and the agency reports unfilled posts within its staff ceiling.Validated
RI-FMW-014@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe issue is not raised as a Chapter 2 finding or requirement in EU material: across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the Commission items on third-country nationals record the temporary residence rule and counts of residence permits, and its 2023 call to register foreigners and give them access to services sits under Chapter 24, so the standard scale was not decisive. The issue's own items describe continuing barriers to third-country workers' access from 2024 to 2026: the migration inspectorate's 2024 proposals to remove problems found in the foreigners law, a 2025 study finding the procedure for employing foreigners bureaucratic, and UNHCR's 2026 finding that only 29 percent of working-age Ukrainian refugees are in paid work, with language, recognition of qualifications and childcare as barriers. The new law on admission of foreigners that would change the rules is a draft due to apply from June 2027.Validated
RI-FMW-014@MDAunresolved_gapopenNo EU item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files states a Chapter 2 requirement on third-country workers, so the gap is judged on the issue's own items. The draft law on admission of foreigners and the draft amendment extending employment services to more categories of foreigners are proposals, and consultation comments on the draft law point to work permits tied to one employer and no clear separation between labour inspection and immigration control, while refugees still face language, recognition and childcare barriers. What remains is a law in force that eases third-country workers' access to the labour market and protects their rights after admission, and support that reaches refugees in practice.Validated
RI-FMW-014@MDApriorityLowThe issue is not raised as a requirement in EU material, which counts residence permits and records the residence rules, and this keeps priority from being High: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Commission recommendation on third-country workers' access to the labour market, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and the 2023 Chapter 24 recommendation on registering foreigners and giving them access to services does not concern employment. The evidence comes from national, international organisation and research sources, which do not raise priority.Validated
RI-FMW-014@MDAtractabilityMediumA full draft law on admission of foreigners and a draft amendment to the employment law have been prepared and consulted, and the employment agency already supports refugees with partner organisations. Against that, the barriers named by UNHCR (language, recognition of diplomas, childcare) need several ministries and funding, and the draft law would apply only from June 2027.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MDAdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceOnly two items fall under this issue: a 2021 Commission finding on use of the online tender platform for COVID-19 procurement and a 2023 report of a regulation requiring most low-value procurement to go through the State Registry of Public Procurement system. Across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the findings that MTender lacks planning and contract management modules and does not offer all procedures concern the replacement of the system and are held under that issue, so no sequence can be drawn on fuller use of the existing modules, and the chapter rating was not used.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MDAunresolved_gapinsufficient_evidenceNo item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files states an EU requirement on fuller use of the existing e-procurement modules or on use of procurement data for red-flag analysis, or reports use of the low-value procurement module required by the 2023 regulation; the Commission's requirements on MTender concern its replacement by a new system. What remains is not known from the evidence held.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MDApriorityLowA search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Commission recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on fuller use of the existing e-procurement modules, since those on MTender concern a new system, and the 2021 finding concerns the transparency of emergency procurement rather than the electronic tools themselves.Validated
RI-TEC-006@MDAtractabilityinsufficient_evidenceThe two items on this issue say nothing about the actors, costs or obstacles involved in fuller use of the e-procurement modules, so tractability cannot be judged.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MDAdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceA search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found that the Commission's only items on these tools are two 2023 calls, in the analytical report and the 2023 report, for electronic platforms and procedures alongside legal alignment on professional qualifications, with no later EU assessment of them. The government's 2025 plans to reconfigure the public services portal as the point of single contact and to link the National Register of Qualifications with Europass are planned and under way respectively, so there is no sequence to judge.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MDAunresolved_gapopenThe 2023 Commission calls for electronic platforms and procedures are met so far only by plans: reconfiguring the public services portal as the point of single contact is planned, and making the National Register of Qualifications interoperable with Europass is under way. What remains is a point of single contact giving service providers full online information and procedures, and an electronic register of regulated professions and qualifications.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MDApriorityLowThe Commission's calls for electronic platforms in this area appear only in 2023, as part of wider recommendations on professional qualifications, and their link to the technology theme is uncertain; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on them.Validated
RI-TEC-007@MDAtractabilityMediumThe public services portal already works and could be reconfigured, and the work lies with national bodies. Against that, one measure is planned and one under way, the government expects possible problems of interoperability with EU platforms, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports past progress on either; the Government describes the EVO portal as a one-stop shop for public services in general, not as the point of single contact for service providers.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingIn 2023 the Commission reported that 67.5% of households had internet at home (58% in rural areas), in 2025 that high-speed broadband reached 57% of the population by mid-2024 while regional disparities persisted, and in 2026 that nearly 95% of households had internet access. The 2026 sub-area wording on 5G deployment, which matches this part of the issue, is some progress, with coverage of 25 to 35%; the Chapter 10 rating was used as context only, as the issue is part of the chapter.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedCoverage and take-up have risen, and the Commission's assessment for the third Reform and Growth Facility release records 6.9% more fixed-broadband connections and faster speeds between 2025 and 2026, but 5G coverage remains well below the EU average and the Reform Agenda describes a rural-urban digital divide. The government counts 431 localities in white areas without fixed broadband, and the plan to develop networks there is proposed and waits for the regulator's geographic survey. What remains is high-capacity fixed and 5G coverage in rural and small localities.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MDApriorityMediumThe rural-urban digital divide is named in a 2024 economic key recommendation on infrastructure investment, the Reform Agenda describes it and the 2026 report rates 5G deployment, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Chapter 10 key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on coverage. The related Reform Agenda step concerns alignment with the Electronic Communications Code, which belongs to another issue.Validated
RI-TEC-013@MDAtractabilityMediumSpectrum was awarded through competitions in 2024 and 2025, operators are investing and the Commission records progress on 5G, which is evidence of past progress. Closing the remaining gaps depends on private operators and on public funding for small, isolated localities, which the government says require significant investment.Validated
RI-TEC-017@MDAdirection_of_travelimprovingIn 2021 the draft data protection law had been awaiting second reading since 2018, and in 2023 the Commission found the law only to some extent aligned with the GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive. The 2024 report recorded adoption of the GDPR law, the 2025 report its entry into force due in August 2026, and the 2026 report its entry into force, the adoption in August 2026 of a law aligning with the Law Enforcement Directive and ratification of the second protocol to Convention 108; the improvement is legal only. The Chapter 10 rating was not decisive, as the issue spans several chapters.Validated
RI-TEC-017@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe main laws the Commission has called for since 2023 are now adopted, but the 2026 report says Moldova should still implement EU standards on contractual clauses between operators and processors, and the 2026 key recommendation still asks for further alignment with EU data protection standards. The order on standard contractual clauses exists only as a draft, and beyond the 2024 and 2026 laws no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports the review of related national laws that the 2023 report described as pending since 2020 and the World Bank recommended in 2024. What remains is the rules on standard contractual clauses and the alignment of related national laws with the new data protection laws.Validated
RI-TEC-017@MDApriorityHighAlignment of data protection legislation is named in the Chapter 10 key recommendations of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, after the 2023 report called for the data protection law to be amended, and it is central to the data theme. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Reform Agenda payment condition on it.Validated
RI-TEC-017@MDAtractabilityHighMoldova adopted the GDPR law in 2024 and, in 2026, the law enforcement data protection law and the ratification of the Convention 108 protocol, which is strong evidence of past progress. What is left is mainly an order on contractual clauses, already drafted, and the alignment of related national laws with the new data protection laws, both within the government's control.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MDAdirection_of_travelinsufficient_evidenceA search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files for the Interoperable Europe Act and the European Interoperability Framework found no Commission finding or recommendation on the national framework's alignment; the EU items are a Growth Plan support measure and a 2026 note that the open data law is in line with the European Interoperability Framework. The government stated in 2025 that the national framework follows the Framework's principles but that the Interoperable Europe Act is not transposed, and drafting of the amending law was announced in February 2026, which is too short a record to show a direction.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MDAunresolved_gapopenBy the government's own account the Interoperable Europe Act has not been transposed, and the law amending Law No. 142/2018 to do so was only initiated in February 2026; the Interoperable Europe factsheet notes that Moldova is not yet part of the European Interoperability Framework data collection. What remains is transposition of the Interoperable Europe Act into the data exchange and interoperability law and alignment of the national framework with the latest European Interoperability Framework.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MDApriorityLowThe issue is not raised as a requirement in the Commission's reports or the Reform Agenda: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no such item, which keeps priority from being High. It rests on the government's own gap analysis and an EU support measure under the Growth Plan.Validated
RI-TEC-027@MDAtractabilityMediumThe change is one amendment to an existing law, prepared by the government, and Moldova already has a working legal and technical interoperability framework. Drafting began only in February 2026, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files shows progress beyond the February 2026 drafting notice.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission reported in 2023 that data exchange through MConnect let the electoral commission check party financing more effectively, but in 2025 it said interoperability between automated verification systems and state registries must still be strengthened, and in 2026 it noted constraints on the full practical functioning of interoperable verification tools. Other sources show connections continuing (336 institutions in 2023 according to SIGMA; 396 integrated state and private systems in 2025 according to the Government, a different measure) while the same underuse is reported: the World Bank in 2024 found interoperability yet to be streamlined, the government in 2025 found systems fragmented, and the data protection authority in 2026 found state bodies still using COI access outside the platform. The Chapter 10 rating was not decisive, as the issue is cross-cutting.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MDAunresolved_gappartly_addressedThe platform and the legal duty to exchange data through it are in place, with sanctions since 2021, and SIGMA found the base registers connected to it in 2023. The data protection authority finds that state bodies still access personal data through COI technology outside the platform, which conflicts with the government's statement that data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, and the Commission in 2026 still finds the interoperable verification tools for asset declarations not fully functioning. What remains is regular use of the platform by all institutions, including an end to access outside it, and full data exchange for asset declaration checks.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MDApriorityMediumInteroperability for asset declaration checks is part of a Chapter 23 Reform Agenda step on the new e-Integrity system, with interoperability ensured through MConnect, is named in the 2025 main findings on Chapter 23 and is repeated as a finding in 2026. These EU items concern only asset declaration checks, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark, key recommendation or Reform Agenda payment condition on use of the platform as a whole, although regular use of the platform is central to the interoperability theme.Validated
RI-TEC-028@MDAtractabilityMediumThe platform, the law and sanctions already exist and connections have grown, which is evidence of past progress. Against that, the remaining problem lies with many institutions that the World Bank says work in silos, and the data protection authority reports that bodies notified repeatedly have still not moved to the platform.Validated
RI-TEC-040@MDAdirection_of_travelpersistentThe Commission found in 2025 that Moldova was not yet fully aligned with the Chips Act and in 2026 that it was yet to align with it. The 2026 sub-area wording on semiconductors, which matches this issue, is some progress, but it rests on the April 2026 law on topographies of semiconductor products, an intellectual property matter outside the issue, so alignment with the Chips Act has not moved.Validated
RI-TEC-040@MDAunresolved_gapopenThe 2026 key recommendation asks for further alignment with the semiconductor acquis, and the government plans to transpose the Chips Act by the end of 2026 but states that there are no national rules on semiconductor production facilities and no responsible institution. What remains is transposition of the Chips Act and the designation and staffing of a competent authority.Validated
RI-TEC-040@MDApriorityMediumAlignment with the semiconductor acquis is a key recommendation in the 2026 report, following a 2025 finding, but only in one report, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on it. The government describes the sector in Moldova as almost non-existent, which makes the issue less central to the theme.Validated
RI-TEC-040@MDAtractabilityLowThe government reports that no institution is responsible for the area, that no ministry employee covers it and that a new post is needed, and the sector is at an early stage. Transposition is planned for the end of 2026, but no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files records progress on the Chips Act itself.Validated

Comparator pilot (run 1b) Validated

CaseCountryIssueDescriptionStatus
CMP-0008ALBRI-TEC-036Albania placed most services on e-Albania, with a 2023 law obliging institutions to use it, and an international source reports high use. Full transactions are not established, payment often fails, and no extracted item shows that the law or the portal caused the reported use.Validated
CMP-0009MNERI-TEC-036Montenegro launched a new portal in December 2024 and a plan for transactional services, but sampled core services were not on it and use on the broad indicator fell before it launched. This case is too early and unverified, and its delivery figures rest on the government's own report.Validated
CMP-0010HRVRI-FMW-015Croatia prepared the European Health Insurance Card before its accession on 1 July 2013: a regulation on the card was adopted in December 2011, the Commission found preparations reaching completion in October 2012, and the Croatian Health Insurance Fund (HZZO) reports issuing the card in 2013 and EU visitors using it. Croatia already had a central health information system (CEZIH), migrated to new hardware in 2012, and by 2013 HZZO was issuing national health insurance cards alongside the EHIC, so the case shows the end state Moldova is working towards rather than how to build the missing preconditions. All statements of results come from HZZO's own reports.Validated
CMP-0011MNERI-FMW-015Montenegro recognises the European Health Insurance Card in its Law on compulsory health insurance but will introduce it only after accession, in wording the Commission repeats in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Asked in 2025 for a feasibility study, it updated one with 2025 data and in February 2026 adopted an action plan for social security coordination that sets out the technical and IT upgrades needed before accession. Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026, but no source in the project links the closure to the card, the card has not been issued and the Commission still asks for the health information system to be adapted.Validated
CMP-0012SRBRI-FMW-015Serbia is a contrast case: the Commission recorded no developments on the European Health Insurance Card, in identical words, in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and in 2025 and 2026 asked Serbia in a key recommendation to develop the IT infrastructure for the card. No Serbian measure on the card's domestic preconditions appears in the evidence, and no source says why the position has not moved.Validated
CMP-0013MNERI-TEC-038Montenegro has had an electronic public procurement system under implementation since January 2021. An independent World Bank assessment requested by the country found in 2023 that the system was a good start but needed substantial upgrading and that old technology limited further upgrading, and the EU assigned funds for an upgrade. The Commission reports improvements to the system in each year from 2023 to 2025, but no source in the project shows that the technology limit was removed or that the system was replaced, and there is no measured result.Validated
CMP-0014MKDRI-TEC-038North Macedonia runs an integrated electronic public procurement system that the Commission describes as functioning efficiently in every report from 2021 to 2026. The portal was upgraded and adapted to a new legal framework by 2020, modules were added in stages, and an updated version was launched on 1 April 2025, with limited progress recorded on it. No source in the project says the earlier system was outdated, so this is a working system being upgraded, not an outdated one being replaced.Validated
CMP-0015MKDRI-TEC-036North Macedonia's national e-services portal, in use since December 2019, reached 338 services by the end of August 2026, including partly available ones, and the Commission reports that its usage rate doubled from the previous year, after the most-demanded certificates went online in 2025. The rise starts from a low level of use, the rate is not defined, and the Commission links it to the new services only by saying that the two went together.Validated

ALN-0035toolingTools and their tests assumed a single run: the tests used the default (latest) run, review pages carried alpha wording, and the alpha's country page linked to index.html after a second run took it.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0036extractionA source already extracted for one run (as a comparator) cannot record a second run's extraction, because an evidence file holds one extraction record.countriesValidated implemented
ALN-0037extractionFirst-pass extractors read only part of long sources (Reform Agenda pages 9 to 26, thesis pages outside the chosen range), so the second pass added 123 items (17 per cent), against a lower share in the alpha.volume; languagesValidated accepted
ALN-0038toolingThe automatic quote check confirms that a quote occurs in the source but not that it ends on a word boundary, so a quote cut mid-word passed (MDA-GOV-2025-002-0467, with an untrue note that the page text broke there).countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0039classificationContradicts links were over-proposed: of 61, an independent check confirmed 8, found 49 apparent (different measures, definitions or reference dates) and 4 not conflicts. Figures that differ because they measure different things were recorded as conflicts.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0040toolingActor records have no field for a successor body and existing rows cannot be edited, so a renamed or merged institution (Bureau for Migration and Asylum and IGM; Ministry of Economy as a former name of ACT-MDA-0004) can only be recorded as a possible duplicate.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0042assessmentParallel issue-judgement batches proposed the same leads_to link when an intervention served issues in two batches, so four links received two conflicting success and attribution pairs; and claims of absence were checked against different counts of the country's items.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0043toolingShared entities let one run's records leak into another run's outputs: a Moldova comparator link from a North Macedonia intervention appeared in North Macedonia's rebuilt RI-TEC-036 brief, and the G6, G6b and outputs builders read every run's judgements, links and queue rows.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0044sourcesHorizontal EU documents (enlargement Communications, Council conclusions) are registered under the first country that used them, so counts, filters, annexes and relevance ratings treated them as that country's documents.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0045assessmentThe priority test was read at G6 with a principle the rules do not state (a fulfilled Reform Agenda condition not repeated in the latest report does not alone make an issue High), and the three-report tests rarely apply to a country with few standard reports.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0046taxonomy matchingShared issue definitions drafted from North Macedonia name features that Moldova's evidence does not show, and six shared issues fit Moldova awkwardly; the risk of anchoring grows with each country.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0047assessmentThe implementation status scale has no value for a law repealed and replaced by a successor, so 'reversed' was used, which reads as backsliding.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0048toolingA one-line append opened decision_log.md for writing before reading it and emptied the file; it was committed and pushed before a package test caught it.countriesValidated accepted
ALN-0049workflowPassing G1, G2, G3, G2b and G5b under a standing instruction, with independent agent checks and the PC-16 limits check, and confirming them at the next decision gate, took the run from G0 to G7 in four days without the late discovery seen in the alpha (ALN-0030).countriesValidated accepted
